title: A stop instruction is not the same as containment.
mainJudgement: A stop instruction is not the same as containment.

committeeQuestion.question: How long does it take to stop a material agent after an intervention decision, and what can still happen during that interval?
committeeQuestion.why: OpenAI reports a 35-second maximum from stop instruction to preventing further model progress in its research environment. That figure excludes detection and decision time and does not reverse completed actions.
committeeQuestion.evidence: A timed test showing detection, decision and enforcement timestamps; the independent control path; actions already queued or completed; and the result when the control service is unavailable.

committeeQuestions.question: Which critical services share the same material provider, and how do we restore the business service when that provider is unavailable?
committeeQuestions.why: APRA warns that common material providers can transmit disruption across institutions. Its system-wide observations do not establish the exposure or recovery capability of any individual firm.
committeeQuestions.evidence: A current service-to-provider map, a severe but plausible disruption test, fallback communications, time to minimum service and unresolved dependencies.

committeeQuestions.question: After patching an exploited internet-facing application, how do we know an attacker’s relay and persistence have also been removed?
committeeQuestions.why: Microsoft describes observed Linux intrusions in which GSocket runs independently of the vulnerable application, so patching alone need not remove access.
committeeQuestions.evidence: A scoped investigation of process ancestry, relay connections and persistence, followed by host remediation and evidence that access has stopped.

judgement.title: A stop instruction is not the same as containment.
judgement.editorialAngle: Use OpenAI’s research-infrastructure stop design and APRA’s shared-provider warning to distinguish detection, intervention and the restoration of business service.
judgement.distinctFromPrevious: Edition 21 tested the time from vulnerability discovery to verified remediation. Edition 22 asks whether an active agent or shared dependency can be contained during execution, including work already queued and actions already completed.
judgement.observation: OpenAI says its Control Room stops further model output within 35 seconds after receiving a stop instruction in its research infrastructure. Separately, APRA says some individual providers support institutions holding more than half of APRA-regulated financial assets.
judgement.executiveJudgement: The two observations describe different environments and neither proves a firm can control its own agents or recover its services. A stop timer begins after someone or something decides to intervene; it does not include detection, human decision-making or the reversal of actions already taken.
judgement.implication: Choose one material agentic workflow and run a controlled stop exercise. Timestamp the alert, decision and independent enforcement; identify actions that remain queued or complete during the interval, then demonstrate the recovery or compensating action for one consequential outcome.

weeklyReadout.heading: Can we stop a material agent and account for what already happened?
steps: Choose one material agentic workflow and define the stop decision.
Timestamp the alert, decision and independent enforcement.
Identify queued and completed actions at the enforcement point.
Demonstrate recovery or a compensating action for one consequential outcome.

topSignals.title: A stop instruction is only one part of agent containment
topSignals.label: OpenAI research infrastructure · provider account
topSignals.why: OpenAI says Control Room can halt further model output within 35 seconds after receiving a stop instruction and denies inference if the control service is unavailable. This is its account of research infrastructure, not proof that completed actions can be reversed or that an enterprise deployment has the same control.

topSignals.title: APRA links AI risk with shared provider dependencies
topSignals.label: Australian prudential supervisor · system outlook
topSignals.why: APRA says AI can create risks within firms and accelerate external threats, while shared material providers can transmit disruption. Some individual providers support institutions holding more than half of APRA-regulated financial assets; this is Australian supervisory evidence, not a measurement of any individual firm’s exposure.

topSignals.title: FINMA sets January start for revised AML requirements
topSignals.label: Swiss supervisor · final ordinance
topSignals.why: FINMA says its revised anti-money-laundering ordinance enters into force on 1 January 2027. The associated self-regulation provides a four-month transition period; affected firms must assess which provisions apply to their own activities.
topSignals.source: Primary / Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority / 2026-11-10

topSignals.title: FSB calls for stronger stablecoin oversight in Türkiye
topSignals.label: FSB peer review · recommendations
topSignals.why: The FSB recommends a dedicated stablecoin regime, stronger supervision and enforcement, and cross-border cooperation in Türkiye. These are recommendations to authorities, not new obligations already imposed on firms.

topSignals.title: GSocket persistence can survive the initial application patch
topSignals.label: Microsoft Security Research · observed activity
topSignals.why: Microsoft describes attackers using an outbound relay after compromising internet-facing applications. Patching the initial flaw does not itself remove the relay client or persistence; the report describes observed telemetry rather than the prevalence of compromise across banks.
